title.rendered: Olori Cecilia Matemilola arrives Owu palace…

content.rendered:
The biography presentation of Her Royal Majesty Olori Cecilia Naadensua Matemilola as a woman whose experience and engagements span education, entrepreneurship, diplomacy, philanthropy and cultural leadership.

A particularly strong aspect of her profile is its international dimension: it connects her Ghanaian royal heritage, Finnish professional experience and her present role as Olori and Queen Consort of Owu Kingdom. Her work in educational development, international relations and Africa–Nordic cooperation gives the biography a broader context beyond ceremonial royalty.
Her Royal Majesty Olori Cecilia Naadensua Matemilola — an international educationist, entrepreneur, philanthropist, diplomat and cultural leader whose work seeks to build bridges between Africa and the Nordic region, while advancing development, women’s empowerment, education and international cooperation.
Congratulations to the Owu Kingdom Abeokuta!

title.rendered: HER ROYAL MAJESTY OLORI CECILIA NAADENSUA MATEMILOLA

content.rendered:
A Profile of Alayeluwa’s New Queen Consort
Her Royal Majesty, Olori Cecilia Naadensua Matemilola, is a distinguished Ghanaian-Finnish international personality whose life and work span education, entrepreneurship, diplomacy, philanthropy and cultural leadership.
Formerly known as Cecilia Naadensua Quarshie, she is a Queen Mother from the Dawurampong-Adjumanku Royal Family of Ghana, an accomplished entrepreneur, author, philanthropist and diplomat. She has also participated in municipal politics in Finland as a former municipal candidate.
With over fifteen years of experience in education and leadership in Finland, Olori Cecilia has distinguished herself through her commitment to educational development and international engagement. She served as the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Ceci Educare Oy, through which she hosted and honoured notable personalities in Finland between 2023 and 2026. Among them were former President of Nigeria, Chief Olusegun Obasanjo; His Royal Majesty, the Olowu of Owu Kingdom; former Vice President of The Gambia, Ousainou Darboe; and former Prime Minister of Finland, Timo Soini.
Her international engagements also extend to diplomacy and global cooperation. She serves as Special Envoy to the Nordic Region for the International Society of Diplomats (ISD) and was the first and only African to serve as a board member of the British Commonwealth Chamber of Commerce in Finland.
A committed philanthropist and advocate of educational empowerment, she has supported beneficiaries across Africa through her educational initiatives, awarding over 20,000 scholarships to individuals in The Gambia, Nigeria, Ghana and other parts of the continent.
Her pioneering presence in international and business organisations has also been remarkable. She was among the first Africans to join the Finnish-Swedish Chamber of Commerce, the Norwegian Trade Association, and the British Commonwealth Chamber of Commerce in Finland. Her contributions have earned her several international awards and recognitions, while her work has received attention in Finland and across the Nordic region, including features in national and international media such as the Helsinki Times.
In Ghana, she is installed as Mputu Hemaa Nana Abena Enyimba II, the Development Queen Mother of Abura in the Oguaa Traditional Area.
She now bears the distinguished title of Her Royal Majesty Olori Cecilia Naadensua Matemilola, Queen Consort of Owu Kingdom, Nigeria.
Her journey represents a meeting point of royal heritage, education, entrepreneurship, philanthropy and international diplomacy. Through her work, she continues to build bridges between Africa and the Nordic region, advancing education, development, women’s empowerment, cultural understanding and international cooperation.
Her Royal Majesty Olori Cecilia Naadensua Matemilola brings to Owu Kingdom a wealth of international experience, cultural depth and a strong commitment to human and societal development.
For further information, search online for:

Cecilia Naadensua Quarshie

title.rendered: Ogogo akulodo, sun re!

content.rendered:
I have come to understand that ageing and sickness can arrive as turning points in life. In what may seem like the twinkling of an eye, the tide changes: the body responds differently, strength may decline, routines are altered, and things once done effortlessly may require caution, patience and assistance.
Yet, for many people, accepting this new reality is difficult. Doubt and denial can delay the conviction needed to begin a new way of living. Until reality is accepted, the necessary coping mechanism may never truly begin.
We age, and sometimes sickness comes, not always gradually enough for the mind to adjust. Life can change in a moment. Wisdom, therefore, is not merely in resisting the change, but in recognising it, accepting it and learning how to live meaningfully within the new reality.
We age and fall sick like the twinkling of an eye; but acceptance gives us the wisdom to adjust, cope and continue living with dignity.
A natural artiste, always in charge—sleep on peacefully. Your artistry and spirit will continue to speak where words can no longer reach. Rest well.
Sincere condolences to the family of late Taiwo Hassan aka Ogogo, a veteran actor and Yewa people. A star dropped…
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR

title.rendered: OLOYE LEKAN ALABI: AN ENDURING ENCYCLOPAEDIA OF IBADANLAND AND YORUBALAND

content.rendered:
Oloye Lekan Alabi was an iconic journalist, author, columnist, publisher and public intellectual whose remarkable life and career left an indelible imprint on Ibadanland, Oyo State and the wider Yoruba world.

He was, in every meaningful sense, an encyclopaedia of the history, people, culture and traditions of Ibadanland and Yorubaland. His extraordinary reservoir of knowledge, memories and experiences made him a valuable repository of the past and a bridge between generations.
Oloye Alabi was not merely a journalist who reported events; he was a chronicler of history and a passionate interpreter of society. Through his writings, publications, public engagements and conversations, he documented personalities, traditions, institutions and defining moments that might otherwise have faded from collective memory.
His life also reflected an uncommon intersection of journalism, scholarship, public service, traditional leadership and statesmanship.
He served as Press Secretary to four governors of the old Oyo State, giving him a rare and privileged perspective on governance, politics and public administration. That experience, combined with his long career in journalism and public relations, enriched his understanding of the evolution of Oyo State and the Nigerian political landscape.
As a distinguished senior traditional chief of Ibadanland, he was equally committed to the preservation and promotion of Yoruba culture. He understood that traditional institutions were not merely ceremonial establishments but custodians of identity, history, values and communal memory.
Oloye Lekan Alabi was therefore much more than a journalist or traditional chief. He was a scholar of Yoruba civilisation, a custodian of culture and tradition, a chronicler of history and a statesman of considerable experience and stature.
His departure created a void, but it did not erase his contribution. The books he authored, the columns he wrote, the histories he preserved, the people he documented and the institutions he served remain part of his enduring legacy.
In the language of our elders, “Agba ki i wa loja, ki ori omo tuntun wo.” When an elder is present, the younger one does not lose his way.
Oloye Lekan Alabi has now joined the ancestors, but the wisdom he gathered and shared continues to guide those who care about the history and future of Ibadanland and Yorubaland.
He lived as a custodian of memory; he departed as a repository of history; and he remains in the collective memory of those whose lives and heritage he documented.
May his memory remain blessed, and may his enduring works continue to illuminate the path for generations yet unborn.
Baami Abese,  o di gba o se!
Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta 
Founder/Coordinator, The SixthSense Initiative and Sixth Sense Series Publications 
Chairman, Association of Nigerian Authors (Ogun Chapter)

title.rendered: From Palace to Policy: The Untapped Power of Traditional Stools

content.rendered:
There was a time when the palace was the first parliament of the people. Before the emergence of modern political institutions, the palace served as the centre of governance, justice, security, diplomacy, economic planning, conflict resolution, and cultural preservation. The traditional ruler was not merely a ceremonial figure; he was the custodian of the people’s welfare, the conscience of the community, and the bridge between the past and the future.

Today, however, many traditional stools have been reduced to symbolic institutions with limited constitutional authority. Yet the challenges confronting our nation—rural insecurity, youth unemployment, declining moral values, environmental degradation, communal conflicts, drug abuse, and weakening family structures—are precisely the areas where traditional institutions possess unmatched influence.

This raises an important question: Are we fully harnessing the power of our traditional stools in national development? The answer is clearly no.

The palace remains the closest institution to the grassroots. Government officials may change after elections, but the palace remains a permanent institution. Traditional rulers understand the history of their people, know the families, appreciate local dynamics, and command moral authority that cannot be legislated.

The Yoruba have long understood this truth. Our elders say:

“Igi gogoro máa wó lójú ọ̀nà, àgbà tó rí i ni yóò kọ́kọ́ ké.”
When a mighty tree is about to fall across the road, it is the elder who first notices and raises the alarm.

Traditional rulers are those elders. They often detect social problems before they become national crises.

Imagine a governance system where every local government actively partners with traditional rulers on community security, environmental sanitation, youth mentorship, agricultural development, educational campaigns, healthcare awareness, and investment promotion. The results would be transformative.

Traditional rulers are not competitors to elected governments. Rather, they are strategic partners whose influence reaches where government bureaucracy often cannot.

The palace can become a policy laboratory.

For instance, campaigns against drug abuse become more effective when supported by respected monarchs and chiefs. Community policing succeeds better when local intelligence flows through trusted traditional structures. Land disputes are often resolved faster through customary mediation than prolonged litigation. Even vaccination drives, census exercises, voter education, and environmental campaigns gain wider acceptance when endorsed by traditional authorities.

One of the greatest strengths of traditional institutions is trust. Trust cannot be manufactured overnight; it is built across generations.

Another untapped asset is cultural diplomacy. Our festivals, arts, language, traditional architecture, crafts, cuisine, and historical sites represent enormous opportunities for tourism and economic development. Palaces should not merely preserve culture—they should become engines of cultural enterprise and local economic growth.

Equally important is the role of traditional rulers in preserving values.

Across many African societies, respect, integrity, honesty, communal responsibility, and compassion were cultivated through the traditional institution. Today, as society grapples with declining values, the palace still possesses the credibility to inspire moral rebirth.

Yet traditional institutions must also evolve.

The modern palace should embrace technology, documentation, research, digital archives, youth engagement, strategic communication, and evidence-based advocacy. Tradition must not become stagnant. As our forebears wisely demonstrated, culture survives not by resisting change but by guiding it.

Traditional rulers should increasingly participate in policy conversations—not partisan politics, but policy development. Their voices should be heard in discussions on education, agriculture, security, climate resilience, urban planning, healthcare, tourism, and social development.

Government, too, has responsibilities. Traditional councils should receive greater institutional support, capacity building, and clearly defined advisory roles. Consultation with traditional rulers should become a deliberate component of policymaking, particularly on matters affecting local communities.

The palace is not an outdated relic. It is a living institution.

As the Yoruba remind us:

“Ilé la ti ń kọ́ ẹ̀ṣọ́ r’òde.”
Charity and strength begin at home.

National development begins with strong communities, and strong communities are sustained by respected institutions.

From palace to policy is not merely a slogan. It is a pathway towards inclusive governance, sustainable development, and lasting peace.

If Nigeria must truly unlock her enormous potential, she must rediscover one of her oldest strengths—the wisdom, legitimacy, and community influence of her traditional stools.

The future of governance will not be built by government alone. It will be built when modern institutions and traditional institutions walk together in mutual respect, shared responsibility, and a common vision for national progress.

As discussed on Ayekoto, a yoruba radio programme on Sweet FM 107.1 Abeokuta.

title.rendered: A Title is Conferred to Recognise Merit, Not to Manufacture it -Orunto Owu

content.rendered:
Before the first title was ever bestowed, character had already been tested. In Yoruba tradition, chieftaincy is not an ornament for vanity but a sacred trust for service. A title does not create integrity; integrity is what makes a person worthy of a title.

Many desire positions and honors without the discipline, maturity, knowledge, and responsibility that such offices demand. They pursue prestige while neglecting the virtues that sustain it. Yet no title, however exalted, can conceal a lack of character forever.
When individuals force themselves into chieftaincy without proper grounding, qualification, or respect for tradition, they often mistake privilege for power. Rather than preserving the dignity of the institution, they reduce it to personal display and misconduct. Such actions diminish not only themselves but also the sacred heritage they claim to represent.
The elders understood this long ago: a title is conferred to recognise merit, not to manufacture it. Chieftaincy is a covenant with the people, the ancestors, and generations yet unborn. It demands wisdom before authority, humility before honour, and service before status.
As the Yoruba say, “Ìwà l’ẹwà”—character is true beauty. Where character is absent, every title becomes an empty shell. Where integrity abides, even without a title, the people will still recognise true nobility.
A kingdom endures not because titles are plentiful, but because those who bear them are worthy of the sacred responsibilities entrusted to them.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: NIGERIA’S “LIONESS OF LISABI” Remembering Chief Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900–1978)

content.rendered:
Many people know Chief Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti simply as the mother of Afrobeat legend Fela Anikulapo Kuti. But long before Fela became famous, she had already secured her place as one of Nigeria’s greatest nationalists, educators, and champions of women’s rights.
Born on 25 October 1900 in Abeokuta, she became the first girl to attend Abeokuta Grammar School before studying in England. On returning home, she devoted her life to education and public service.
In 1946, she founded the Abeokuta Women’s Union (AWU), which grew into one of the most influential women’s movements in colonial Nigeria. She led thousands of women in peaceful campaigns against unfair taxation and discrimination under British colonial rule.
Her famous demand was:
“No Taxation Without Representation.”
She believed that women should not be taxed while being denied a voice in government. Her leadership during the Egba Women’s Tax Revolt (1947–1948) became one of the most significant acts of peaceful resistance in Nigeria’s colonial history. The sustained protests eventually led to the suspension of the tax on women and marked a turning point in the struggle for justice in Egbaland.
For her courage, she earned the traditional title Beere (“First Among Equals”) and became widely known as the “Lioness of Lisabi.”
Her influence extended beyond Abeokuta. In 1947, she was the only woman in the Nigerian delegation that travelled to Britain to challenge the Richards Constitution. She later participated in discussions that led to the Macpherson Constitution of 1951 and continued campaigning for voting rights and greater political participation for Nigerian women, including those in Northern Nigeria.
Funmilayo also argued that before British colonial rule, Yoruba women enjoyed greater economic and political influence, owning property, trading independently, and participating in public affairs. She dedicated her life to protecting those rights.
Her outspoken activism attracted criticism and political opposition, but she remained committed to justice, equality, and democratic participation. Her work inspired generations of Nigerians, including her son, Fela Kuti, whose music carried the same spirit of resistance against injustice.
On 18 February 1977, during the military raid on Kalakuta Republic, she sustained serious injuries. She never fully recovered and passed away on 13 April 1978, aged 77.
Sadly, many newspapers announced her passing with the headline:
“Fela’s Mum is Dead.”
History, however, remembers her for far more than that.
Chief Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was not just the mother of a music icon. She was one of the architects of modern women’s activism in Nigeria, a fearless nationalist, and a woman whose courage helped reshape the nation’s history.
Her legacy continues to inspire Nigerians and Africans who believe in justice, equality, and the power of peaceful civic action.
Nigeria will always remember her as the “Lioness of Lisabi”
By Oluwafemi Omodara

Funmilayo also argued that before British colonial rule, Yoruba women enjoyed greater economic and political influence, owning property, trading independently, and participating in public affairs. She dedicated her life to protecting those rights. Her outspoken activism attracted criticism and political opposition, but she remained committed to justice, equality, and democratic participation. Her work inspired generations of Nigerians, including her son, Fela Kuti, whose music carried the same spirit of resistance against injustice. On 18 February 1977, during the military raid on Kalakuta Republic, she sustained serious injuries. She never fully recovered and passed away on 13 April 1978, aged 77. Sadly, many newspapers announced her passing with the headline: “Fela’s Mum is Dead.” History, however, remembers her for far more than that. Chief Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was not just the mother of a music icon. She was one of the architects of modern women’s activism in Nigeria, a fearless nationalist, and a woman whose courage helped reshape the nation’s history. Her legacy continues to inspire Nigerians and Africans who believe in justice, equality, and the power of peaceful civic action. Nigeria will always remember her as the “Lioness of Lisabi” By Oluwafemi Omodara

title.rendered: New Omoniinu Owu Kingdom Abeokuta-Chief Adewale Quadri

content.rendered:
Omooba Rasheed Adewale Adesupo Quadri was born on the 16th of November 1967 to Dr Olukayode Aderemi Quadri, a prince of both Fusengbuwa and Fidipote ruling houses of Ijebu Ode and Princess Dr Mrs Moninuade Adegbeminiyi Quadri, Erelu Gbogboade of Owu kingdom. A distinguished son whose life journey reflects dedication, enterprise, and an enduring commitment to service, community, and excellence.
He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Geology, a discipline that provided him with a solid foundation in understanding the earth, its resources, and their value to human advancement. In his quest for broader impact, he further obtained a Postgraduate Diploma in Management, equipping him with strategic insight, leadership acumen, and the ability to navigate complex business environments.
He began his professional career in the oil trading sector, where he demonstrated strong commercial awareness, integrity, and a deep understanding of global energy markets. He subsequently expanded into third-party logistics, contributing to efficient supply chain operations and earning a reputation for reliability and excellence.
In alignment with his academic background and passion for resource development, he established Geopetra Resources Limited, a mining consultancy committed to advancing responsible mineral exploration and supporting small-scale mining initiatives. Through this enterprise, he has contributed to unlocking economic value while promoting sustainable practices within the sector.
With a forward-looking vision, he also founded Quad Solutions Ltd, through which he delivers IT consulting and digital transformation services. Leveraging his expertise in governance, risk, and compliance, he supports organisations in strengthening their systems, enhancing resilience, and aligning with global standards.
Beyond his professional accomplishments, he remains deeply rooted in community and service. He is a devoted member of NASFAT, where he upholds values of faith, discipline, and societal contribution. He is also an active member of the Royal Crest Club, a body known for its commitment to educational development and community advancement in Ijebu and Remo lands. In addition, he belongs to Egbe Jagunmolu Okunrin Fehintade Akile Ijebu, an esteemed age-grade association that fosters unity, cultural heritage, and collective responsibility among its members.
In further demonstration of his commitment to youth and education, the maiden edition of the Omoniinu Foundation Essay Writing and Debate Competition was successfully held in March this year, bringing together secondary schools across Owu. This initiative, which is set to become an annual event, reflects his passion for nurturing young minds, promoting intellectual engagement, and inspiring the next generation toward excellence.
Across all spheres of his life, he has distinguished himself as a man of vision, discipline, and integrity. His journey is a testament to the power of knowledge, resilience, and purposeful enterprise.
Today, as he is adorned with this honour, we celebrate not only his achievements but also his unwavering commitment to the progress of his people and the betterment of society. He stands as a worthy son, an ambassador of excellence, and a shining example of what can be achieved through dedication and service.
-The SixthSense Initiative outreach

title.rendered: The Cultural Nuances of Drums in Traditional Settings: Chieftaincy Ceremonies and the Language of Dance

content.rendered:
In African traditional societies, particularly among the Yoruba, the drum is far more than a musical instrument. It is a language, a herald, a historian, and a sacred medium through which culture speaks. During chieftaincy ceremonies, drums announce honour, proclaim lineage, preserve history, and direct the movement of both the titled and the untitled. To understand a traditional ceremony without understanding its drums is to hear the sound but miss the message.
Every chieftaincy title carries its own identity, and that identity is reflected in its drumming. Skilled drummers know the praise names (oríkì) of families, lineages, towns, and chiefs. Through rhythmic patterns and talking drums, they recount ancestral achievements, victories, virtues, and responsibilities. The drum reminds a chief that a title is not merely a privilege but a covenant with history.
Dance in a chieftaincy ceremony is therefore not entertainment alone. It is a visible response to the drum’s message. Every dignified step acknowledges ancestry, honours the throne, and affirms the legitimacy of the occasion. The chief does not simply dance because music is playing; he dances because the drum has called him into communion with his forebears and with the people he has sworn to serve.
Among the Yoruba, different drums carry different responsibilities. The Dùndún speaks in tonal language, echoing praise poetry and royal greetings. The Bàtá possesses deep spiritual significance and commands reverence through its complex rhythms. The Gángan, the talking drum, imitates human speech, delivering messages that only trained ears fully comprehend. The Ìgbìn is associated with sacred rites and ancient traditions, while other ensembles mark celebration, procession, or solemnity. Each drum has its place, its voice, and its protocol.
A knowledgeable dancer listens before moving. The rhythm determines posture, pace, and expression. A royal dance is measured and restrained, reflecting dignity rather than exuberance. An elder’s dance demonstrates wisdom and composure. A warrior’s dance conveys courage and readiness. Thus, dance becomes a language of character, while the drum becomes its interpreter.
The relationship between the drummer and the chief is one of mutual respect. The drummer must understand palace etiquette, genealogy, and ceremonial protocol. He knows when to praise, when to pause, and when silence itself is the greatest honour. Likewise, the chief recognises the drummer as a custodian of memory, for many family histories survive not in books but in the rhythmic language preserved across generations.
The timing of drumming is equally significant. The drum announces arrivals, accompanies processions, welcomes distinguished guests, signals moments of homage, and celebrates the conferment of titles. It distinguishes one phase of the ceremony from another, ensuring that every action unfolds in harmony with tradition.
Sadly, modern ceremonies sometimes reduce drumming to mere entertainment, encouraging excessive display and competitive dancing. Such practices risk diminishing the sacred dignity of traditional institutions. When dance becomes a contest for attention rather than an expression of honour, the cultural philosophy behind the ceremony is weakened.
Our forebears understood that the drum educates as much as it entertains. It teaches history, reinforces values, celebrates integrity, and reminds every chief that leadership is rooted in service, humility, courage, and accountability. The rhythm of the drum is, in many respects, the heartbeat of the community itself.
As a Yoruba proverb reminds us: “Bí ìlù bá dákẹ́, ìjó á dáwọ́ dúró.” — “When the drum falls silent, the dance comes to an end.” This saying extends beyond music. When culture loses its voice, identity begins to fade. The preservation of traditional drumming is therefore the preservation of memory, authority, and civilisation.
Every beat of the drum carries the footsteps of our ancestors. Every dignified dance pays homage to those who came before us. Every chieftaincy ceremony should remind us that culture is not inherited by chance; it is preserved through understanding, discipline, and reverence.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: Before the Obas: The Origin of the Title “Oba” and the Crowning of Ajíbọ̀sìn

content.rendered:
Long before colonial rule and long before the country now known as Nigeria of January 1, 1914 came into existence, great civilisations flourished across West Africa. Among the most enduring institutions created by these civilisations is kingship, symbolised in Yorubaland by the revered title Oba.
Yet an important question deserves careful reflection: When did the title “Oba” become institutionalised, and what form of leadership existed before it?
According to the ancient traditions of the Owu Kingdom, the formal institution of the title Oba followed the crowning of Ajíbọ̀sìn, who is remembered as the first Olowu to receive the sacred crown directly from Odùduwà at Ilé-Ifẹ̀. This event is regarded in Owu tradition as a defining moment in the evolution of Yoruba kingship.
Before this sacred institution, leadership in many communities was exercised through councils of elders, clan heads, spiritual authorities, accomplished warriors, and respected community leaders. Authority was earned through wisdom, age, military prowess, and religious responsibility rather than through the fully developed institution of crowned monarchy.
Within Yoruba civilisation, the word Oba came to signify far more than a political ruler. The Oba became the custodian of the people’s history, traditions, customs, sacred institutions, and collective identity. The crown represented both temporal authority and spiritual responsibility.
Yoruba oral tradition holds that Odùduwà established the royal institution at Ilé-Ifẹ̀, from which many royal dynasties trace their origin. His descendants are traditionally associated with the establishment or influence of numerous kingdoms, including Owu, Oyo, Ijẹbu, Ondo, Owo, Ekiti, and others.
The Owu Kingdom preserves the tradition that Ajíbọ̀sìn’s coronation occupies a foundational place in this history. This account remains central to Owu historical consciousness and illustrates the kingdom’s enduring claim as an ancient pillar of Yoruba civilisation.
While historians continue to study the evolution of Yoruba kingship using archaeology, linguistics, and documentary evidence, oral tradition remains an indispensable source for understanding the worldview and historical memory of the Yoruba people.
Today, the title Oba continues to embody authority, service, justice, cultural continuity, and the sacred responsibility of preserving the heritage of the ancestors for generations yet unborn.
Owu l’Àkọ́dà—Owu is the pioneer. In the consciousness of Owu tradition, the crowning of Ajíbọ̀sìn stands as a defining milestone in the institutional history of Yoruba monarchy.
This version clearly distinguishes Owu traditional history (“According to the ancient traditions of the Owu Kingdom…”) from claims that are universally established by historians. That distinction strengthens the credibility of the publication while preserving the importance of Owu’s historical narrative.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: OLOTA WAS CROWNED 200YEARS BEFORE ALAKE

content.rendered:
The paramount ruler of Egbaland, Oba Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo had reiterated that the Olota of Ota, Oba Abdulkabir Obalanlege and residents of Ota were under the prescribed authority of Alake.
Responding to the asssertion in a statement, which he personally signed, Oba Obalanlege said that “Though I am presently on official assignment in Switzerland, I need to remind Alake of Ake that in Ogun State, the settlement of Awori people preceded the establishment of Abeokuta as an Egba Kingdom in 1830. Otta, the foremost Awori town within the present Ogun state and which is the industrial nerve centre, for instance,  has been existing since the 15th century.”
The Ota monarch added in the statement that the first Olota, Oba Ikoriku Toribo was coronated in 1621, while the first Alake in Abeokuta,  Sagbua Okukenu was crowned on 8th August,  1854.
According to him, “it goes without saying that putting an Olota under an Alake is both a traditional misnomer and historic fallacy.
“The Ife palace, where the crowns came from knows better! Never  in history has Otta been captured by the Egbas, rather we rescued them from Oyo invasion.”
While arguing that all Ota territories were under his authority, Alake of Egbaland, Oba Adedotun Gbadebo stressed that Ota land was a conquest territory by Egbaland in 1917, and that Ota and it’s environs were under the then Egba Native Administration and the Alake.
It would be recalled that, the Olota of Ota, Oba Abdulkabir Obalanlege had penultimate week through the Olota-in-council accused Alake of Egbaland of installing non-Aworis as royal fathers in Aworiland of Ogun State.
Oba Obalanlege through the Seriki of Ota, Bashorun Olanrewaju argued that, the Olota of Ota is the prescribed traditional authority over all lands, towns and villages with the suffix, Ota, including Sango, Gbalefa and all others.
But the Alake-in-council on Friday emphasized that, Ota, Sango, Iju, Gbalefa, Abule Lemomu, Oke-Ore, Adekoyeni, Atan among others were part of lands and settlements captured by the Egbas during war against Ado-Odo in 1843.
He added that, between 1853 and 1900, Ota was ruled by the Egbas through their Residents representatives which till date made the Olota of Ota a member of the Egba traditional council.
He said that despite series of courts’ decisions on issues brought against Alake’s position in all Egba physical and geographical areas which reconfirmed the legal and traditional jurisdiction of Egbaland on Ota districts, the Olota of Ota and his chiefs resorted to self-help.
“For those who have little or no knowledge about Ota and its environs or district, between 1900 and now, the Ota people were within the prescribed authority of the Alake. For instance, it was Oba Gbadebo I, the Alake, that appointed Oba Aina Ako, the Olota in 1901.
“So, Ota and Gbalefa districts from the early time were all under the then Egba Native Administration and the Alake. Ota historically, administratively and through right of conquest of 1841 fell on Egba Administration as part of Egbaland. The Olota of Ota, Oba Abdulkabir Adeyemi Obalanlege, is currently an active member of the Egba Traditional Council.
“We are worried that, the Olota and his Chiefs have been involving themselves in self-help by engaging in violent visits to Egba towns and villages within Gbalefa, Iju, Atan, Ijoko, Itori, Sango and others.“
Alake therefore called on the Ogun State Commissioner of Police to intervene in the excesses and one-sided activities of the police instigated harassment of the Egba indigenes.
Culled Kabiyesitv (2019)

He said that despite series of courts’ decisions on issues brought against Alake’s position in all Egba physical and geographical areas which reconfirmed the legal and traditional jurisdiction of Egbaland on Ota districts, the Olota of Ota and his chiefs resorted to self-help. “For those who have little or no knowledge about Ota and its environs or district, between 1900 and now, the Ota people were within the prescribed authority of the Alake. For instance, it was Oba Gbadebo I, the Alake, that appointed Oba Aina Ako, the Olota in 1901. “So, Ota and Gbalefa districts from the early time were all under the then Egba Native Administration and the Alake. Ota historically, administratively and through right of conquest of 1841 fell on Egba Administration as part of Egbaland. The Olota of Ota, Oba Abdulkabir Adeyemi Obalanlege, is currently an active member of the Egba Traditional Council. “We are worried that, the Olota and his Chiefs have been involving themselves in self-help by engaging in violent visits to Egba towns and villages within Gbalefa, Iju, Atan, Ijoko, Itori, Sango and others.“ Alake therefore called on the Ogun State Commissioner of Police to intervene in the excesses and one-sided activities of the police instigated harassment of the Egba indigenes. Culled Kabiyesitv (2019)

title.rendered: The secret of traditional knowledge lies in its demonstration through writing, speaking, and living it.

content.rendered:
Culture reveals itself to those who deliberately seek its wisdom. Through the counsel of elders, participation in communal activities, observation of customs, and reverence for tradition, one gains not just information but true cultural experience.
Reading, research, and the careful study of our past events, histories, and practices remain invaluable sources of traditional knowledge. A people who neglect their history gradually lose their identity.
As a traditional leader and custodian of our heritage, I shall continue to document, teach, and demonstrate these enduring values. It is my duty to promote, preserve, and protect our traditions, culture, and customs, so that future generations may inherit not only our stories but also the wisdom that has sustained our people through the ages.
Heritage preserved is identity secured.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom

Through the counsel of elders, participation in communal activities, observation of customs, and reverence for tradition, one gains not just information but true cultural experience. Reading, research, and the careful study of our past events, histories, and practices remain invaluable sources of traditional knowledge. A Chief Abiodun Lasile highlights the importance of preserving traditional knowledge through research, writing, teaching, and daily practice. He emphasizes that culture, history, and customs are the foundations of identity and must be faithfully passed on to future generations.

title.rendered: DEEP REFLECTION

content.rendered:
Why do I seem to attract so much hatred and resentment? Why are hatred and ill will so heavily directed at me?
— Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR
This question has occupied my thoughts over time.
To the best of my ability, I have chosen the path of truthfulness. I have striven to live uprightly, lifted others without asking for a reward, supported genuine causes, and devoted myself to selfless service. These are not occasional acts; they have become my way of life.
Yet, despite these efforts, some people remain committed to gossip, falsehood, resentment, and unwarranted hostility. Such behaviour, however, has neither diminished my resolve nor hindered my progress. If anything, it has strengthened my conviction that purpose must never be abandoned because of opposition.
The Yoruba elders wisely remind us:
“Igi tó bá ga, afẹ́fẹ́ ló máa ń kọ́kọ́ lù.”
The tallest tree is the first to be struck by the wind.
And again:
“Bí ènìyàn bá ń ṣe rere, kò túmọ̀ sí pé gbogbo ènìyàn yóò fẹ́ràn rẹ.”
Doing good does not guarantee that everyone will love you.
I have therefore resolved to remain steadfast in good character, for reputation built on truth outlives rumours built on envy. Gossip fades, but integrity endures. Hatred is temporary, but a life of purpose leaves a legacy.
My successes and unprecedented achievements have not been stopped by those who speak behind my back. Instead, they have reaffirmed a timeless truth: when one’s path is guided by sincerity, diligence, and divine grace, opposition may slow the journey, but it cannot stop the destination.
My prayer is “May my life continue to be defined not by the voices of detractors, but by the enduring testimony of my character and service.”
-Chief Abiodun Oladimeji Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: Traditional Workshop at Apomu

content.rendered:
Traditional Workshop for the Kingmakers of Apomu, facilitated by the Iwarefa of Owu Kingdom, Abeokuta, was a profound gathering dedicated to strengthening the institution of traditional leadership through knowledge, wisdom, and cultural responsibility.
A kingdom endures not merely because of its throne, but because those entrusted with its customs understand the sacred weight of their duties. Àṣà ni ìpilẹ̀ ìjọba; ẹni tí ó bá sọ àṣà nù, a sọ ìtàn ara rẹ̀ nù—culture is the foundation of every kingdom; whoever abandons it also abandons their own history.
This capacity-building workshop reaffirmed the need to institutionalise our traditional processes correctly, preserve our customs faithfully, and pass our heritage to future generations without dilution. The wisdom of our forebears remains our greatest compass, for a people without memory cannot secure their tomorrow.
May our royal institutions continue to flourish in truth, dignity, and the enduring spirit of Yoruba civilisation.
In attendance; Alapomu, Obamaja, Orunto, Osupori, Olosii, Olori Ituns and the elected Apomu kingmakers
— Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR
Orunto Baalufe, Owu Kingdom, Abeokuta

title.rendered: Yorùbá proverbs have remained flawless. -Orunto Owu

content.rendered:
Yorùbá proverbs have remained flawless through the ages because they are distilled wisdom, tested by time and affirmed by experience. They are not mere sayings; they are enduring principles that guide conduct, preserve values, and illuminate the path of life.
Our forebears chose observation as one of the most potent methodologies of inquiry. They watched nature, studied human behaviour, listened to the rhythms of society, and drew lasting conclusions from lived experience. From these careful observations emerged proverbs that have outlived generations and continue to speak with remarkable relevance.
Indeed, Yoruba proverbs are observatory postulations—philosophical conclusions born from the patient observation of life. As the elders say, “Àgbà tó rí ohun tí ọmọ kò rí, bí ọmọ bá gun orí igi tó ga, kò lè rí i.” An elder sees what the youth cannot, even from the top of the tallest tree. Such is the depth of wisdom that observation bequeaths.
When a people faithfully observe life before speaking, their words become timeless. That is why Yoruba proverbs continue to serve as moral compasses, intellectual treasures, and cultural beacons from one generation to another.
Over the years, I have deliberately devoted myself to studying Yoruba proverbs and wise sayings, paying close attention to their meanings in order to deepen my understanding of life and humanity. They have become the guiding principles of my thoughts, decisions, and worldview.
As a traditional leader, I have found this timeless reservoir of indigenous wisdom invaluable. It continually shapes my judgment, enriches my leadership, and reminds me that the wisdom of our ancestors remains a reliable compass for navigating the complexities of the present age.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: Owu Kingdom is with Character, Tradition and Institutions -Orunto Owu

content.rendered:
A kingdom does not endure merely because a throne stands or a crown is worn. Its true strength lies in the character, wisdom, and discipline of those entrusted with preserving its customs, traditions, and institutions. The throne is visible to the eyes, but culture is the unseen pillar that bears its weight. When the custodians of tradition faithfully uphold the values handed down by their forebears, the kingdom flourishes; when they neglect them, even the grandest palace begins to lose its meaning.

The Owu Kingdom of Abeokuta stands today not simply because history remembers it, but because generations of kings, kingmakers, chiefs, and devoted sons and daughters have deliberately preserved its identity despite displacement, wars, and changing times. From the tragic destruction of Orile Owu to the rebuilding of the kingdom in Abeokuta, the survival of Owu has been a testimony to the resilience of a people who refused to let their heritage perish. Our history teaches that kingdoms are rebuilt with courage, but they are sustained by culture.

The institution of the Iwarefa, together with the kingmakers and traditional title holders, carries a sacred obligation that extends beyond the installation of an Olowu. They are guardians of ancestral wisdom, custodians of sacred rites, interpreters of customs, protectors of justice, and transmitters of values from one generation to the next. Their responsibility is not ceremonial; it is spiritual, moral, and historical.

The Yoruba have long declared: Àṣà ni ìpilẹ̀ ìjọba; ẹni tí ó bá sọ àṣà nù, a sọ ìtàn ara rẹ̀ nù. Culture is the foundation upon which every kingdom stands; whoever abandons culture abandons the story of his own existence. A people without memory become strangers in their own land, but a people who honour their heritage remain firmly rooted regardless of the changing winds of time.

For Owu Kingdom, preserving culture is not an exercise in nostalgia. It is the deliberate preservation of identity, dignity, and continuity. Every festival, every traditional title, every palace protocol, every proverb, every drumbeat, every greeting, every oral tradition, and every sacred rite forms part of the living archive of our civilisation. These are not relics of the past; they are instruments for shaping the future.

As custodians of Owu heritage, we therefore have a solemn duty to institutionalise our traditions correctly, document our history faithfully, educate the younger generation diligently, and ensure that the wisdom of our ancestors continues to illuminate the path of those yet unborn. In doing so, we preserve not only the throne of the Olowu but also the soul of the Owu Kingdom itself.

For when culture is preserved, the kingdom lives. When wisdom is transmitted, the people remain united. When tradition is honoured, history continues to speak. And when every generation faithfully receives and hands over the sacred trust of its ancestors, the legacy of Owu Kingdom endures forever.

-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR

title.rendered: Lamine Yamal: A Lesson in Gratitude and Perspective

content.rendered:
Spanish football star Lamine Yamal has shown that true greatness is measured not only by talent but also by humility and gratitude.
Reflecting on the expectations placed upon him, Yamal remarked that he does not see football as “pressure.” Instead, he points to the real struggles endured by his parents. He has spoken about his mother giving birth to him as a teenager and his father working difficult jobs to provide for the family, saying that those sacrifices represent genuine pressure. Compared to their experiences, he considers playing football to be a privilege.
Born and raised in Rocafonda, a working-class neighbourhood in Mataró, Spain, Yamal comes from a family of immigrant heritage. His mother is from Equatorial Guinea, while his father is from Morocco. Despite financial hardship, his parents supported his dream, leading to his development at FC Barcelona’s La Masia Academy, where his extraordinary talent flourished.
Yamal has never forgotten his roots. His now-famous “304” goal celebration honours the last three digits of Rocafonda’s postal code, symbolising pride in the community that shaped him.
His story is a powerful reminder that behind many outstanding achievements are parents and guardians whose quiet sacrifices make success possible. The applause often goes to the star, but the true foundation of greatness is laid by those who endure hardship so that the next generation can dream, grow and succeed.

content.rendered:
“A three-eyed stranger cannot see more than a one-eyed native.”
-Orunto Baalufe Owu
Among the Yorùbá, we say that wisdom does not dwell in the loudest voice, but in the one who knows where the ancestors planted the first iroko. A traveller may possess three eyes, yet he cannot see beyond the one eye of the child born and nurtured on the soil of his forebears.
The history of the Owu Kingdom in Abeokuta is not a garment woven overnight, neither is it a market tale to be altered by every passer-by. It is an inheritance received from our ancestors, guarded by our royal institutions, preserved in oral tradition, affirmed in documented history, and carried in the hearts of generations.
He who has not drunk from the ancient stream cannot truly describe its source. Àlejò kì í mọ ibi tí òkúta ti ń yọ omi. A stranger does not know where water springs from the rock. Likewise, àgbà kì í wà l’ọ́jà kí orí ọmọ tuntun wọ. When elders are present, history should not be turned upside down by ignorance.
Those who seek to narrate Owu history without understanding its sacred foundations are like hunters pursuing the rainbow. However far they travel, they will return with empty hands, for truth does not reveal itself to those who chase appearances instead of knowledge.
Our heritage is ancient. Its roots reach into the earliest foundations of Yorùbá civilisation and the enduring legacy of Odùduwà. Such a history is not sustained by sentiment but by memory, scholarship, tradition, and the unwavering testimony of those entrusted with its preservation.
Let every seeker of truth approach with humility, for bí a bá fẹ́ mọ ìtàn ìlú, a máa béèrè lọ́wọ́ àwọn tí ìlú bí. If one truly desires to know the history of a people, one must learn from those whom the land itself has nurtured.
I speak not to quarrel, nor to seek approval. I speak because the ancestors entrusted this heritage to our care. We owe them truth, and we owe posterity an undiluted account of who we are.
I remain a proud son of Owu Abeokuta. While others may speak from conjecture, I shall continue to speak from inheritance, preserving, protecting, and proclaiming the enduring legacy of our fathers. For àṣà ni ìpilẹ̀ ìjọba; ẹni tí ó bá sọ àṣà nù, a sọ ìtàn ara rẹ̀ nù—culture is the foundation of every kingdom, and whoever abandons it also abandons the story of his own existence.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: Do Not Build Your Life Around a Passing Season

content.rendered:
The elders say that no harmattan lasts forever, and no rainy season refuses to give way to sunshine. The earth has its seasons, and so does life.
A wise person does not build a permanent house on temporary ground. He does not celebrate prosperity as though it will never fade, nor does he surrender to hardship as though dawn will never come.
The yam planted in the rainy season is not harvested on the same day. The river that swells with the rains will one day return to its banks. So it is with fortune and adversity—they are both visitors, not permanent residents.
Therefore, build your life on character, not on circumstances; on wisdom, not on wealth; on honour, not on applause. Character outlives seasons, and integrity does not wither with changing times.
When the season changes, only those whose roots are deep remain standing. The person who understands this walks with humility in abundance and with hope in adversity, knowing that every season has its purpose and every condition has its appointed end.
Do not build yourself around a temporary season. Build yourself around timeless values, for seasons pass, but character endures.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR

title.rendered: I do not look back.

content.rendered:
Lions do not turn back because dogs bark. They remain focused on the path ahead, undistracted by the noise behind them.
My eyes are fixed on the future, my mind on greater exploits, and my steps on higher accomplishments.
I have witnessed many hurdles, yet I remain standing. Every challenge has strengthened my resolve and sharpened my purpose.
As a leader, my responsibility is to provide direction, coordinate people and resources, and make decisions that advance the vision. No minor distraction can derail my thinking or diminish my focus.
I have always understood that leadership demands courage. Leaders are called to make difficult decisions, not to seek universal approval. While others may be distracted by the noise, a true leader remains steadfast in purpose, guided by wisdom, conviction, and integrity.
The noise behind me will never determine the direction before me. I remain focused, I remain resolute, and I move forward toward greater exploits.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta.

title.rendered: SixthSense SmartWords…. Feyikogbon

content.rendered:
Among the Yoruba, envy is regarded as a poverty of the heart, not a lack of possessions. The envious are seldom many, for ìwà búburú kì í pọ̀ l’ọ́jà—evil character never becomes the way of the majority.
Our elders teach that the truly prosperous person is not the one who owns the most, but the one whose heart rejoices at another’s success. The envious, however, cannot celebrate another’s blessings. They are troubled by another person’s honour, disturbed by another’s progress, and pained by another’s peace.
Such people are recognised in every community. They smile with their lips while their hearts burn with bitterness. They covet not only another’s wealth but also another’s position, influence, reputation, and sometimes even the life that Providence has graciously bestowed upon that person.
That is why the wise keep a respectful distance from those consumed by envy, for our fathers say: “Àrùn ojú kì í jẹ́ kí ẹni rí ire ẹlòmíràn.” (The sickness of envy prevents a person from seeing another’s blessings with a clear heart.)
A community flourishes where people celebrate one another, for another person’s light does not diminish your own. As another Yoruba saying reminds us, “Oorun kì í dín kù nítorí pé ó tan ìmọ́lẹ̀ sí ilé ẹlòmíràn.” (The sun loses nothing by shining on another’s home.) It is contentment, good character (ìwà pẹ̀lẹ́), and gratitude—not envy—that preserve families, kingdoms, and society.
The SixthSense Initiative is a registered NGO hugely promoting children reading culture and human capacity development.
Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

aioseo_head_json.description: Among the Yoruba, envy is regarded as a poverty of the heart, not a lack of possessions. The envious are seldom many, for ìwà búburú kì í pọ̀ l'ọ́jà—evil character never becomes the way of the majority. Our elders teach that the truly prosperous person is not the one who owns the most, but the Chief Abiodun Lasile reflects on the Yoruba understanding of envy as a poverty of the heart, emphasizing the values of contentment, gratitude, good character, and celebrating the success of others as foundations for personal fulfillment and social harmony.

title.rendered: The Sacred Trust of an Elder in the Yoruba Worldview

content.rendered:
In the Yoruba worldview, old age is not merely a measure of years; it is a sacred trust earned through character, wisdom, and integrity. An elder is expected to be the living conscience of the community, one whose words carry the weight of truth and whose conduct inspires confidence.
Our forebears taught that “Òtítọ́ ni ìpìlẹ̀ ayé”—truth is the foundation upon which life stands. Therefore, for an elder to knowingly tell lies is regarded as a profound moral failing, one capable of diminishing not only personal honour but also the dignity of age itself. While every human being is capable of error, an elder preserves honour not by denying a mistake but by embracing the truth with courage and humility.
The Yoruba also remind us that “Àgbà kì í wà l’ọ́jà, kí orí ọmọ tuntun wọ́.” The presence of elders should prevent confusion, falsehood, and moral disorder. Likewise, “Ọ̀rọ̀ àgbà kì í ṣubú lásán” teaches that the words of an elder are expected to be thoughtful, truthful, and worthy of lasting respect.
The Omolúàbí ideal places elders on a lofty moral pedestal. They are not revered simply because they have grown old, but because they are expected to embody the virtues that justify such reverence—truthfulness, fairness, self-restraint, honour, and wisdom. An elder may err, for no human being is infallible, but to persist in falsehood is to betray the very essence of elderhood.
As custodians of our heritage, we must uphold this timeless standard. The greatest legacy an elder leaves behind is neither wealth nor power, but a name associated with truth, honour, and unquestionable integrity. For when an elder speaks, the community should hear not merely a voice advanced in age, but the enduring echo of truth itself.
This version reflects the enduring philosophy of the Yoruba Omolúàbí tradition while acknowledging that elders are human, yet held to a higher moral standard because of the responsibility that comes with age and leadership.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: The Honour of Elders in Yoruba Tradition

content.rendered:
In traditional Yorubaland, truthfulness is one of the highest virtues expected of an elder. It is considered a grave moral failing—almost a taboo—for an elderly person to be found telling lies or living a life of falsehood.
Elders are revered as custodians of wisdom, integrity, and moral authority. They are expected to be above reproach, honourable in conduct, and exemplary in character. Their words are meant to inspire confidence and command respect. Even when an elder makes a mistake, our culture expects such a person to acknowledge it with dignity rather than resort to falsehood, for nothing diminishes an elder’s honour more than being known as a liar.
This is one of the enduring values of the Yoruba Omolúàbí ethos. It places our elders on a moral pedestal, recognising that age should be accompanied by truthfulness, wisdom, and honour. Such standards have long served as the foundation of trust, respect, and social harmony within our families and communities.
As we preserve our cultural heritage, we must also preserve this noble expectation—that our elders remain worthy examples of integrity for younger generations to emulate.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

As we preserve our cultural heritage, we must also preserve this noble expectation—that our elders remain worthy examples of integrity for younger generations to emulate. -Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR  Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: ….privilege of participating in several strategic gatherings dedicated to the advancement of Egbaland

content.rendered:
Let us keep the conversation alive about the future of Egbaland, working together with all stakeholders to preserve our rich heritage and build a stronger, more prosperous community.”*
— Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR
Orunto Baálùfẹ̀, Owu Kingdom, Abeokuta
The year 2025 has afforded me the privilege of participating in several strategic gatherings, lectures, and forums dedicated to the advancement of Egbaland. Each engagement has reinforced the importance of collaboration, visionary leadership, cultural preservation, and sustainable development.
Among these engagements were:
  • The Ogun Central Coronet Obas and Baales Meeting at the June 12 Cultural Centre, Abeokuta.
  • The Egba Education Roundtable at OOPL, Abeokuta.
  • The Egba Legacy and Preservation Summit, organised by the Youth Wing of the Ogun Central chapter of the National Youth Council of Nigeria (NYCN), Abeokuta.
  • The Sobo Sowemimo Annual Lecture at the Abeokuta Club.
These conversations must not end in conference halls. They should inspire practical actions, strengthen partnerships, and encourage every Egba son and daughter to contribute meaningfully to the future of our land.
Our heritage is our identity, our unity is our strength, and our collective commitment will determine the legacy we leave for generations yet unborn.
Let us continue the conversation—and, more importantly, let us continue the work.
Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

content.rendered:
When an individual goes to great lengths to trace the rainbow in a traditional circle merely to denigrate a people of history, heritage, and importance, it raises legitimate concern about the underlying motive.
Such conduct should not be dismissed as mere coincidence or eccentricity. It deserves careful observation and thoughtful reflection—not to provoke unnecessary reactions, but to remain guided, guarded, and discerning. Both the immediate actions and the long-term pattern should be considered with wisdom rather than emotion.
As I have often said, “Calculated patience is not weakness; it is the wisdom to wait for the right moment to act.” – Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR
Owu Abeokuta remains a Kingdom—steadfast in its history, rich in its heritage, and confident in its identity. Its enduring legacy cannot be diminished by mischief or deliberate distortion.
History stands on truth, and truth outlives propaganda.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta

title.rendered: Odùduwà and the Installation of Ajíbọ̀sìn: The Beginning of the Owu Monarchy

content.rendered:
According to the cherished oral traditions of Owu and the broader Yoruba historical heritage, Odùduwà, the revered progenitor and unifying ancestor of the Yoruba people, established Ajíbọ̀sìn as the first Olowu following the founding of the Owu Kingdom. This tradition forms one of the enduring pillars of Owu identity, preserving the sacred link between the royal institution of Owu and the earliest era of Yoruba civilisation.
Like much of early Yoruba history, this account has been faithfully transmitted through generations by oral tradition rather than written records. Consequently, no precise calendar date can be assigned to the installation of Ajíbọ̀sìn. However, the convergence of oral traditions with historical and archaeological scholarship places this formative period of Yoruba state formation between the 10th and 12th centuries CE.
For the Owu people, the enthronement of Ajíbọ̀sìn was more than the appointment of a ruler; it represented the establishment of an enduring monarchy founded on legitimacy, custom, courage, and the shared values of the Yoruba nation. The Olowu stool has since remained a symbol of continuity, resilience, and the rich cultural heritage that has distinguished Owu through the centuries.
While historical scholarship continues to examine the chronology of early Yoruba kingdoms, the Owu tradition remains steadfast in affirming that Ajíbọ̀sìn was the first Olowu, installed by Odùduwà himself at the dawn of the Owu Kingdom—a legacy that continues to inspire pride among the descendants of Owu today.
Owu Kingdom, the first and legitimate by the progenitor.
-Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR
Orunto Baalufe, Owu Kingdom, Abeokuta

title.rendered: Ajíbọ̀sìn and His Lineage in Owu Tradition

content.rendered:
According to the cherished oral tradition of the Owu people, Ajíbọ̀sìn, the first Olowu of Owu, was the son of Ìyúnadé, a granddaughter of Odùduwà, the revered progenitor of the Yoruba people. This maternal lineage places Ajíbọ̀sìn within the royal house of Odùduwà and affirms the legitimacy of the Owu monarchy from its very inception.
Owu tradition further maintains that Odùduwà personally entrusted Ajíbọ̀sìn with the establishment of the Owu Kingdom and installed him as its pioneer monarch. To ensure the stability of the new kingdom, he appointed the Ìwàrẹ́fà—the six principal chiefs—to accompany the young monarch as guardians of the kingdom, custodians of tradition, military commanders, and administrators of the emerging state.
This genealogy is of profound significance in Owu historical consciousness. It reflects not only a familial connection to the house of Odùwà but also the constitutional and spiritual legitimacy of the Olowu dynasty. Through Ajíbọ̀sìn, the Owu Kingdom traces its royal heritage directly to the founding lineage of Yorubaland, a tradition that has been preserved across generations through oral history, royal customs, and the enduring institution of the Olowu.
Owu l’akoda
-Chief Abiodun Lasile, DL, MnbR
Orunto Baalufe, Owu Kingdom, Abeokuta

title.rendered: What an Aso Rock Business Model!

content.rendered:
I am convinced that every public speech has an audience and should reflect the realities of that audience.
The Akara and Kulikuli proposition may have been appropriate as a survival strategy in the remotest communities of an earlier era, but it falls far short of the aspirations of 21st-century Nigerian women. After decades of advocacy for women’s empowerment—from the Better Life Programme to the landmark Fourth World Conference on Women—our conversations should be centred on access to quality education, affordable healthcare, entrepreneurship, technology, decent jobs, and sustainable economic opportunities.
How can women struggling under the weight of inflation, rising transport costs, and declining purchasing power be inspired by suggestions that merely reinforce subsistence living, especially when such advice comes from the comfort of the nation’s highest corridors of power?
The issue is not whether selling akara or kulikuli is an honourable business—it certainly is. The concern is whether such examples represent the level of economic vision Nigerians deserve at a time of deep hardship.
Economic reforms may be reflected in statistical reports, but the true measure of success is whether ordinary citizens experience relief in their daily lives. Until the benefits are felt in the markets, on the streets, and around family dining tables, many Nigerians will continue to question whether those figures reflect their lived reality.
Leadership communication should not only acknowledge hardship; it should inspire confidence through practical, scalable solutions that restore dignity, expand opportunity, and improve the quality of life for all Nigerians.
-Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR

title.rendered: Spirits eat Akara!

content.rendered:
Akara selling is as old as the Yoruba people themselves. It is an honourable and legitimate trade that has sustained families for generations. There is nothing new or revolutionary about it. Spirit eats Akara!
The concern is not with akara or those who earn an honest living by selling it. The concern is that, in the twenty-first century, public policy and national leadership should be focused on creating an environment where viable industries, modern enterprises, innovation, and productive investments flourish—not presenting age-old subsistence occupations as solutions to widespread economic hardship.
Women should not be perpetually confined to the lowest rung of the economic ladder or encouraged to remain in a cycle of subsistence living. The goal of leadership should be to empower women with access to education, finance, technology, entrepreneurship, and opportunities that lift families out of poverty, not policies or narratives that inadvertently normalize impoverishment.
The nation’s commonwealth exists to expand opportunities and improve the quality of life of its people, not to institutionalise survival while those entrusted with public resources enjoy the privileges of power.
Dis Akara thing dey make me write!
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR

title.rendered: What an Aso Rock Business Model!

content.rendered:
I am convinced that every public speech has an audience and should reflect the realities of that audience.
The “Akara and Kulikuli” proposition may have been appropriate as a survival strategy in the remotest communities of an earlier era, but it falls far short of the aspirations of 21st-century Nigerian women. After decades of advocacy for women’s empowerment—from the Better Life Programme to the landmark Fourth World Conference on Women—our conversations should be centred on access to quality education, affordable healthcare, entrepreneurship, technology, decent jobs, and sustainable economic opportunities.
Beyond Survival: Why Nigerian Women Need Opportunities, Not Just Subsistence Strategies
How can women struggling under the weight of inflation, rising transport costs, and declining purchasing power be inspired by suggestions that merely reinforce subsistence living, especially when such advice comes from the comfort of the nation’s highest corridors of power?
The issue is not whether selling akara or kulikuli is an honourable business—it certainly is. The concern is whether such examples represent the level of economic vision Nigerians deserve at a time of deep hardship.
Economic reforms may be reflected in statistical reports, but the true measure of success is whether ordinary citizens experience relief in their daily lives. Until the benefits are felt in the markets, on the streets, and around family dining tables, many Nigerians will continue to question whether those figures reflect their lived reality.
Leadership communication should not only acknowledge hardship; it should inspire confidence through practical, scalable solutions that restore dignity, expand opportunity, and improve the quality of life for all Nigerians.
-Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR

title.rendered: ANA MARKS 80TH BIRTHDAY OF FEMI OSOFISAN WITH LANDMARK COLLOQUIUM ON AFRICAN THEATRE, PERFORMANCE TRADITION By ANA Media Team

content.rendered:
As part of activities marking the 80th birthday celebration of renowned playwright, scholar, and former President of the Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA), Emeritus Professor Femi Osofisan, scholars, writers, and theatre practitioners gathered on June 22, 2026, at the Wole Soyinka Theatre, University of Ibadan, for a landmark colloquium on African Drama and Performance Traditions: The Past, The Present and The Future.
Organised by the Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA), the event also featured the launch of an anthology, goodwill messages, award presentations, and a series of tributes, reinforcing Osofisan’s enduring influence on African literature, theatre, and cultural scholarship.
The colloquium drew a distinguished audience of academics, literary figures, theatre practitioners, and stakeholders from Nigeria’s creative and cultural sectors. Among those present were Professor Remi Raji, former and 10th President of ANA; Professor Wumi Raji; Professor Diran Ademiju-Bepo; Professor Gbemisola Adeoti; Dr. Sola Adeyemi; the Director-General of the Nigerian Copyright Commission (NCC), Dr. John Asein; and Mr. Tosin Akeredolu, Acting Executive Secretary of the Reproduction Rights Society of Nigeria (REPRONIG), who represented the Chairman of the REPRONIG Board, Mr. Adedapo Gbadega.
In his address as Guest of Honour, the President of ANA, Dr. Usman Oladipo Akanbi, paid tribute to Emeritus Professor Femi Osofisan, describing him as one of the foremost pillars of the Association. He noted that the celebration was both a recognition of Osofisan’s towering contributions to literature and theatre and an acknowledgment of his impactful tenure as the third President of ANA, during which he strengthened institutional structures and inspired new directions for the Association.
A goodwill message was also delivered on behalf of Dr. Wale Okediran, Secretary-General of the Pan African Writers Association (PAWA). The message celebrated Osofisan’s immense contributions to African literature and theatre and acknowledged his historic role as the pioneer President of PAWA, whose leadership helped shape the continental organisation’s vision and mission in its formative years.
Delivering the keynote address, Emeritus Professor Olu Obafemi (FNAL, NNOM, D.Litt. Hon.) situated African drama within a continuum of history, performance, and imagination. Speaking on the theme African Drama and Performance Traditions: The Past, The Present and The Future, he traced African theatre to indigenous ritual and performance forms such as festivals, storytelling, music, dance, and masquerade traditions like Egungun and Alarinjo.
He described African theatre, drawing on Wole Soyinka’s theatrical philosophy, as a “dome of continuity” linking ancestors, the living, and future generations. While acknowledging the disruptions introduced by colonialism and European theatrical frameworks, he highlighted the resilience and adaptability of African performance traditions through travelling theatre movements and modern literary drama.
Professor Obafemi further examined modern African theatre as a tool of cultural reclamation, political resistance, and social transformation, giving special attention to Femi Osofisan’s dramaturgy. He noted that Osofisan’s works reimagine myth, history, and folklore to confront oppression and amplify marginalised voices. He concluded by calling for a decolonised, technologically responsive African theatre rooted in indigenous languages, digital innovation, and community engagement.
The colloquium also featured a robust panel session moderated by Professor Remi Raji, with contributions from leading scholars across Nigeria and abroad.
Professor Wumi Raji (Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife) opened the panel with Femi Osofisan: Tradition and Transformation, highlighting Osofisan’s ability to bridge indigenous cultural traditions with modern theatrical forms through the creative reinterpretation of folklore and history.
Professor Diran Ademiju-Bepo (University of Jos), in Revolutionary Aesthetics in African Drama and Performance Traditions: Beyond Femi Osofisan?, examined the continuing relevance of Osofisan’s radical artistic vision and its influence on newer generations of dramatists.
Professor Mabel Evwierhoma (University of Abuja), in Decolonisation of Performance in Dire Seasons for Today or Tomorrow? FO and the Eye of the Future, emphasised Osofisan’s role as a visionary dramatist challenging colonial structures while imagining new futures for African performance.
Professor Gbemisola Adeoti (Obafemi Awolowo University) presented Eto Rooo!: Reviewing Indigenous African Sources of Osofisan’s Drama, tracing the Yoruba oral traditions, folklore, music, and ritual performance forms that underpin Osofisan’s dramaturgy.
Dr. Sola Adeyemi (University of East Anglia, United Kingdom), in Reclaiming Tradition, Confronting Power, Imagining Futures: African Theatre Through Osofisan, examined Osofisan’s theatre as a space of cultural recovery and political engagement.
Professor Steve Inegbe (University of Uyo), in Navigating Performance Spaces in Two Plays Directed by Femi Osofisan: The Artist as a Humorist, focused on Osofisan’s use of humour, satire, and inventive staging in addressing socio-political issues.
Professor Emmanuel Emasealu (University of Port Harcourt) also delivered a scholarly presentation that further underscored the depth and continuing relevance of Osofisan’s dramatic oeuvre.
A major highlight of the event was the presentation and official launch of the anthology Garlands for the Dream-Seeker, edited by Denja Abdullahi and Ezekiel Fajenyo. The collection brings together poetic tributes from Nigerian and African writers in honour of Osofisan’s eight-decade journey as a writer, scholar, and cultural icon, also known by his poetic name, Okinba Launko.
In his foreword, ANA President Dr. Akanbi described the anthology as “a resounding testament and a verbal libation poured in honour of greatness,” noting that it reflects the admiration of colleagues, students, mentees, and literary communities across generations.
The event also featured the formal presentation of an award to Emeritus Professor Femi Osofisan in recognition of his outstanding contributions to literature and his enduring support for ANA.
Other memorable moments included the cutting of the 80th birthday cake, led by Dr. John Asein of the NCC alongside the ANA President, and the unveiling of a painted portrait of the celebrant by artist Olumide Sowumi, which drew widespread admiration.
Anchored by Dr. Tunde Awosanmi, the colloquium combined scholarship, celebration, and artistic expression in honour of one of Africa’s most influential dramatists.
The celebrations will be rounded off today with a special art exhibition in honour of Professor Osofisan at the Odunlade Art Gallery, Ibadan, providing yet another platform to celebrate his remarkable legacy and contributions to African arts and culture.
The event ultimately reaffirmed Femi Osofisan’s towering legacy in African literature, theatre, and intellectual discourse, while also providing a platform for renewed reflection on the future of African drama and performance traditions in a rapidly changing world.

aioseo_head_json.description: As part of activities marking the 80th birthday celebration of renowned playwright, scholar, and former President of the Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA), Emeritus Professor Femi Osofisan, scholars, writers, and theatre practitioners gathered on June 22, 2026, at the Wole Soyinka Theatre, University of Ibadan, for a landmark colloquium on African Drama and Performance Traditions: The Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA) celebrated the 80th birthday of Emeritus Professor Femi Osofisan with a landmark colloquium at the University of Ibadan, featuring scholarly discussions on African theatre, performance traditions, cultural heritage, decolonisation, and the future of African drama.

title.rendered: Owu Kingdom Abeokuta is a kingdom of great minds, noble heritage, and enduring values

content.rendered:
Our strength does not lie in envy, resentment, or bitterness toward others. Rather, it lies in our confidence in who we are, our history, and our contributions to society.
We are not an embittered people driven by jealousy. We celebrate achievement wherever it is found and remain proud of our unique identity, culture, and traditions. Those who choose the path of resentment and needless antagonism often become disgruntled, self-defeated, and disillusioned, losing sight of the opportunities that unity, purpose, and self-development provide.
The Owu spirit teaches dignity, industry, resilience, and progress. We build rather than destroy, preserve rather than diminish, and contribute rather than complain. Our focus remains on strengthening our heritage, empowering future generations, and advancing the collective good of our people and humanity at large.
Owu Oduru, Omo aji f’epe s’ere
-Chief Abiodun Lasile DL MnbR 
Orunto Baalufe Owu Kingdom Abeokuta
